solution: Let x_i say whether island i holds treasure. A surviving value b_i = d forbids treasure strictly closer than d, i.e. on the whole interval [i-d+1, i+d-1], and separately requires treasure at i-d or at i+d. Mark the union of all forbidden intervals in O(n) with a difference array, then greedily place treasure on every position that was not forbidden: this is the pointwise-maximal candidate set, it satisfies all the forbidding constraints by construction, and since extra treasure can only help the 'nearest is at exactly distance d' requirements, it is valid whenever any set is valid. Finish by recomputing every island's nearest-treasure distance with a two-pass prefix/suffix sweep and comparing it against the surviving values, printing -1 on any mismatch; whenever the check passes the set is automatically nonempty, since an all-forbidden line means some constraint had both of its candidate positions forbidden. O(n) per test case. Equivalently the constraints are unit clauses (not x_j) plus binary clauses (x_{i-d} or x_{i+d}), so a 2-SAT solver also solves it, which is what the judge tags suggest. Verified exhaustively over all b arrays for n <= 6 and on 20000 random cases against a 2^n brute force, and it reproduces all twelve sample verdicts.
annotator: claude agent, verified against a brute force
